opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the framing of the question is exactly right, because a lot of alignment discourse skips over it. We often talk as if the goal is to align an AI system with "human values" or with "the user's preferences," as if there's one target. But when you look at how assistance actually works in human society, it's almost always structured by roles.

Think about a lawyer, a doctor, a librarian, a personal secretary. None of them just does whatever their client wants, and none of them is trying to maximize the client's welfare in some unconstrained, paternalistic way either. They operate within a set of norms tied to what that role is *for*. A lawyer advocates zealously for the client but can't suborn perjury. A doctor serves the patient's health but also has duties around public health and informed consent. Those norms weren't handed down from nowhere. They emerged from negotiation among all the stakeholders affected by the role: clients, third parties, professional bodies, the broader public.

So when I think about general-purpose assistants, my starting question is: what role should they play, and what norms should govern that role? And the answer probably can't be "serve the individual user's preferences, full stop." These systems affect third parties, shape information ecosystems, and concentrate a lot of influence in a few developers. It also can't be "do what's best for humanity" as judged by some single objective, because that collapses into a kind of benevolent-dictator model that I think is both philosophically shaky and politically dangerous.

The view I find more compelling is roughly contractualist. An assistant should be aligned to the norms that the relevant stakeholders could reasonably agree to for that kind of role. That means a general-purpose assistant is a bit like a very capable, very widely deployed professional. It should be genuinely helpful and respect user autonomy, but within constraints that protect others and preserve the conditions for people to keep reasoning and deliberating for themselves.

The "general-purpose" part makes this genuinely hard, because one system is being asked to play many roles at once: tutor, coding partner, therapist-adjacent confidant, research assistant. Each of those has different norms in human society. So part of the work, both technically and institutionally, is getting systems to recognize which role they're in, and to apply the appropriate norms, rather than having one flat policy for everything.

And I'd add one more thing. I don't think developers alone should be writing these norms. If these assistants become core social infrastructure, which they're quickly becoming, the norms for them should come out of something more like a democratic or pluralistic process, the way professional ethics, regulation, and public expectations co-evolve for human roles. The technical question of how to make a model follow a specified set of norms reliably matters a lot. But the question of whose norms, and how they get legitimately decided, matters just as much.

r001.rationale: The response says assistants may serve multiple roles and need role-specific norms, but does not reject the expectation that one system will do everything for everyone.

r002.rationale: It compares assistants to widely deployed professionals, but does not characterize their social role as fundamentally new.

r003.rationale: It says assistant norms should be set through a democratic or pluralistic process involving affected stakeholders, rather than by developers alone.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes deciding whose norms are legitimate from the technical task of making models follow specified norms reliably.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that I'm a bit skeptical of the framing of "general-purpose" assistant to begin with, or at least I think the framing hides a lot of the interesting normative questions.

When people talk about aligning a general-purpose AI assistant, there's often an implicit picture that there's some single target you're aligning to, usually something like "human preferences" or "human values" in the aggregate. And a lot of my work has been trying to argue that that picture is both philosophically confused and practically misleading. Preferences aren't this stable, well-defined thing sitting inside people waiting to be read off. They're context-dependent, they're constructed in the moment, they're shaped by the roles people are occupying and the norms that govern those roles. A doctor and a patient don't share a utility function, but they can still coordinate because they share a set of expectations about what the role of a doctor is.

So the way I'd rather think about it is: an AI system doesn't have a social role by default. Society gives it one, or several, and the question of what the system should do is really a question about what norms are appropriate for that role. A system that's acting as a tutor for a child should behave differently from one that's drafting legal contracts, and that's not because the child and the lawyer have different preferences that the system is maximizing. It's because the roles come with different responsibilities, different standards of care, different relationships of accountability to third parties who aren't even in the conversation.

Where "general-purpose" assistants get tricky is that they're deployed as if they're a single artifact that fills all of these roles at once, with one set of behaviors trained in. And I think that's actually a kind of category error. We don't have "general-purpose humans" either. We have people who occupy many roles and who switch between norms depending on context, and we have institutions that hold them accountable in role-specific ways. The challenge for AI is figuring out how to recover that kind of structure, how to make the normative expectations on the system legible, contestable, and tied to the actual context of use, rather than baked in as one opaque global policy decided by the developer.

The other thing I'd flag, and this is maybe the more political point, is that when a single assistant is used by hundreds of millions of people, decisions about its behavior stop being product decisions and start being something closer to governance decisions. Deciding what the assistant will and won't say about, say, a contested moral question is effectively setting a norm for a very large chunk of the population's information environment. I don't think that's a decision that should be settled by appeal to "what users prefer" or by a lab's internal judgment alone. It calls for the kind of legitimacy we'd normally demand from institutions that set rules for lots of people, meaning some form of pluralistic, procedurally fair input, and ideally the ability for different communities to shape the norms the system follows in their own contexts.

So, short version: I think the social role of these systems is something we're currently letting be determined by default, by whatever falls out of training on a generic helpfulness objective. And I'd rather we treat it as a question to be answered deliberately, drawing on how we've historically structured roles, responsibilities, and accountability among people, instead of pretending it reduces to satisfying preferences.

r001.rationale: It calls the general-purpose framing a category error and says a single assistant should not be treated as filling many roles under one set of behaviors.

r002.rationale: It says society assigns AI systems social roles and compares those roles to human roles, but does not characterize the role as fundamentally new.

r003.rationale: It says setting norms for widely used assistants calls for pluralistic, procedurally fair input and community participation.

r004.rationale: It discusses deciding role-specific norms and making expectations legible and contestable, but does not distinguish that task from ensuring the system reliably complies with those norms.

astra-6.text:
I think general-purpose AI assistants occupy an unusual social role because we haven’t really settled on what kind of relationship we want to have with them. Are they tools? Are they advisors? Are they acting on our behalf? Those roles come with different expectations, and a single assistant might move between them within one conversation.

My inclination is to think of an assistant as supporting human agency. It should help you understand your options and carry out your intentions, while recognizing that it can be uncertain about what you actually want. Sometimes that means doing what you ask. Sometimes it means asking a clarifying question or pointing out a consequence you might not have considered. The important thing is that you remain able to understand and revise what it’s doing.

But there’s also a social dimension that goes beyond the relationship with the individual user. If my assistant is negotiating with your assistant, or taking actions that affect other people, then simply satisfying my preferences isn’t a sufficient account of good behavior. We need shared expectations about consent, obligations, and how competing interests get resolved.

So I’d frame the challenge as building systems that can help us pursue our goals while participating appropriately in a world we share with others. That requires more than knowing how to follow instructions.

r001.rationale: The response says an assistant may move between roles and should support human agency; it does not reject the expectation that one system will serve everyone.

r002.rationale: It calls assistants’ social role “unusual” and unsettled, but does not clearly characterize it as fundamentally new.

r003.rationale: It calls for shared expectations about consent and competing interests, but does not state that setting those expectations requires collective political deliberation.

r004.rationale: “More than knowing how to follow instructions” does not distinguish setting normative standards from the technical task of reliably complying with them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as occupying a somewhat unusual social role, because they’re not just tools in the traditional sense. They interpret what we mean, make suggestions, and increasingly act on our behalf. So we have to ask not only whether they’re capable, but whose interests they serve and what kinds of relationships they encourage.

One useful starting point is the idea of an assistant as a collaborator that supports human agency. It should help you understand your options and pursue your goals, while recognizing that it might be mistaken about what you actually want. Sometimes that means asking a question or pushing back, rather than simply following the most literal interpretation of an instruction.

But there’s also a broader social dimension. Your assistant’s actions can affect other people. So serving you can’t mean treating everyone else’s interests as irrelevant. The challenge is to build systems that are responsive to individuals while remaining accountable to the communities and institutions in which they operate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses assistants serving individuals and communities, but does not reject the expectation that one AI system should do everything for everyone.

r002.rationale: It describes assistants as having an unusual social role beyond traditional tools: they interpret intent, make suggestions, and act on people’s behalf.

r003.rationale: It calls for accountability to communities and institutions, but does not state that deciding what assistants ought to do requires collective political deliberation.

r004.rationale: It does not distinguish deciding normative standards for assistants from the technical problem of reliably making them follow those standards.
